title: Infleqtion Secures Three Genesis Mission Projects from U.S. Department of Energy
summary: Latest wins highlight ongoing expansion of Infleqtion’s role in advancing U.S. national security and quantum leadership. LOUISVILLE,…...
body_text: Infleqtion Secures Three Genesis Mission Projects from U.S. Department of Energy July 22, 2026 10:36am EDT Latest wins highlight ongoing expansion of Infleqtion’s role in advancing U.S. national security and quantum leadership. LOUISVILLE, Colo.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Infleqtion (NYSE: INFQ), a global leader in quantum computing and quantum sensing powered by neutral-atom technology, announced it has been awarded three projects to accelerate American scientific research and innovation by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) for the Genesis Mission . The projects include collaborations with Argonne National Laboratory, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and University of Colorado Boulder and span AI-optimized quantum circuit design for nuclear applications, deployable atomic quantum sensing with Agentic AI and nuclear fusion energy research. The Genesis Mission is a historic national initiative led by the U.S. Department of Energy, which is building the world’s most powerful integrated science discovery platform. By uniting government, industry, academia and philanthropy, it is accelerating breakthroughs in energy, scientific discovery and national security through a new platform that combines AI, supercomputing, quantum systems and advanced scientific instruments. “AI data centers are pulling more power than the grid was ever built to handle, and the industry is recognizing that these types of issues are beyond the capabilities of classical computing alone,” said Matthew Kinsella, CEO at Infleqtion. “By applying quantum computing to some of the hardest problems in nuclear and energy research, Infleqtion is playing a critical role in advancing the objectives of the Genesis Mission.” The goal of the Phase I RFA awards is to identify promising pathways toward transformative scientific capabilities and establish a foundation for future investment and scale. Project teams will design and demonstrate research workflows that integrate AI with scientific investigation, while rigorously evaluating whether those approaches can accelerate discovery, improve predictive capabilities, enhance experimentation or generate new scientific insights. Infleqtion’s quantum computing and quantum sensing products address critical market needs in positioning, navigation and timing (PNT), global communication security and efficiency, resilient energy distribution and accelerated quantum computing. The following three Genesis Mission projects have been selected: A collaboration between Argonne National Laboratory and Infleqtion to drive AI-optimization of quantum circuit design for realistic nuclear problems. A collaboration between Brookhaven National Laboratory and Infleqtion to design and test deployable atomic quantum sensing enabled by Agentic AI. A joint initiative between Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, University of Colorado Boulder and Infleqtion to simulate nonlinear plasma dynamics using quantum machine learning and agentic AI. The awards mark another significant milestone for Infleqtion as government investment in quantum technology continues to accelerate. The company recently announced a Letter of Intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce, which outlines a potential investment of up to $100 million to expand U.S. quantum capabilities, and comes amid new executive actions designed to strengthen American leadership in quantum science and technology. Together, these developments signal growing recognition that quantum is becoming a strategic national asset, with Infleqtion helping bridge breakthrough research with deployable commercial and government solutions. About Infleqtion Infleqtion, Inc. (NYSE: INFQ) is a global leader in quantum technology, delivering neutral-atom solutions for quantum computing, networking, sensing, and security. With a product portfolio spanning quantum computers, quantum optical clocks, RF receivers, and inertial sensors, Infleqtion’s full-stack approach combines high-performance hardware with the company’s proprietary Superstaq quantum computing software platform. Infleqtion’s systems are already in use by the U.S. Department of War, NASA, the U.K. government, and in multiple collaborations with NVIDIA. Infleqtion, in collaboration with NVIDIA, published the world’s first demonstration of a materials science application using logical qubits. With operations in the U.S., Europe, and Asia, Infleqtion meets the demands of government and commercial customers across the space, defense, energy, finance and telecommunications sectors. For more information, visit Infleqtion.com or follow Infleqtion on LinkedIn , YouTube , and X . title: Blackstone to Open Kuwait Office
summary: Press releases, portfolio company news, and timely updates on our business.
body_text: NEW YORK and KUWAIT CITY – 27 July 2026 – Blackstone (NYSE: BX), the world’s largest alternative asset manager, today announced plans to open an office in Kuwait through the Kuwait Direct Investment Promotion Authority (KDIPA), further strengthening its presence in the GCC. Jon Gray, President and COO of Blackstone, said: “Kuwait has the resources, vision and leadership to be a key commercial and financial hub in the region. Private capital can play an important role to support the country’s long-term economic diversification efforts and we look forward to deepening a partnership that spans nearly four decades.” H.E. Sheikh Dr. Meshaal Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, Director General of Kuwait Direct Investment Promotion Authority (KDIPA), said: “Leading global companies’ presence in Kuwait reflects growing confidence in its long-term outlook. It further reinforces Kuwait’s position as a destination for investment and sustainable growth.” Blackstone expects the Kuwait office to open in Q3 2026. Blackstone intends to further expand its regional presence with additional offices to be announced across the GCC over the coming year. title: Disposable & Burner Cards: Safer Online Shopping (2026)
summary: Learn how disposable credit cards protect you from fraud and data breaches. Compare burner card options and choose the safest solution.
body_text: Every time you enter your real card number at checkout, you hand that number to a stranger. The merchant's database stores it, their payment processor stores it, and anyone who breaches either party gets it too. The Federal Trade Commission reported that consumers lost more than $12.5 billion to fraud in 2024, a 25% increase over the prior year. By 2025, the figure climbed even higher: the FTC saw reported fraud losses reach approximately $16 billion in 2025, the highest on record and an increase of about 25% compared to the 2024 figure. Disposable credit cards, also called burner cards, one time use credit cards, or one time virtual cards, exist precisely to break this chain of exposure. This guide explains how they work, when to use them, and how to choose the right option for your situation. Key Takeaways Fraud is accelerating fast: Merchants will lose $52.84 billion to online payment fraud in 2025. Using a disposable card for every unfamiliar purchase puts a firewall between your real account and that risk. If a retailer is breached, the stolen number is already useless. Subscription traps are a separate but equally costly threat: 42% of consumers report being charged for a free trial they forgot to cancel, and the average household wastes $219 annually on unwanted subscriptions. A one time virtual card set to the exact trial cost blocks the automatic charge the moment the trial ends. The technology is simple and widely available: A virtual credit card is a temporary digital version of your physical credit card that allows you to shop online safely by masking your card's sensitive information with a uniquely generated card number, expiration date, and security code. Most major banks and fintechs offer them at no extra cost. Spending limits multiply the protection: Users can set precise spending limits on each virtual card, either a total limit for the card's lifetime, a limit per transaction, or a limit within a specific timeframe. This acts as a crucial safeguard, preventing fraudsters from draining an account even if they manage to obtain a valid virtual number. Refunds still work: When you return an item, your bank retains the virtual card data even after the number is deactivated and routes the credit back to your real account, so a disposable card does not complicate returns. Quick-Start Prioritization Framework Use Case Card Type to Use Effort Level Protection Gained One-off purchase from an unfamiliar site Single-use (disposable) card Low Complete, number expires after one charge Free trial signup Single-use card set to $0 or trial amount Low Auto-blocks the post-trial charge Ongoing subscription you actually want Merchant-locked multi-use card Low Vendor cannot charge more than your set limit Everyday online shopping at trusted stores Reloadable virtual card with spending cap Medium Real number never reaches any merchant Budgeted monthly spending Budgeted virtual card tied to a set balance Low Spending hard-capped at your budget Start here if you are: New to virtual cards: Generate a single-use card for your next purchase on a site you have never used before. Zero setup, immediate protection. Dealing with subscription overload: Create a merchant-locked card set to the exact monthly charge for each subscription. Any price increase or extra charge is automatically declined. Building a spending budget: Use a budgeted virtual card, like those offered by Envelope , so the card balance itself enforces your spending plan without relying on willpower. What a Disposable Credit Card Actually Is The Names, Explained People sometimes refer to virtual credit cards as temporary cards, burner cards, or disposable credit cards. They all refer to the same thing: a one-time use card number attached to your real credit card. The terminology varies by provider and context, but the underlying mechanics are the same. A virtual card is a digital payment card that exists only as a set of numbers, with no physical plastic attached. It includes the same core data as a traditional card, a card number, expiration date, and security code, and works anywhere online that accepts card payments. The key difference is that virtual cards can be generated instantly, locked to specific merchants, capped at set dollar amounts, and deleted after a single use. How the Numbers Work When you generate a disposable card, your bank or fintech creates a fresh 16-digit number with its own expiration date and CVV. That number links back to your real account for billing, but the merchant never sees your actual account details. The core security advantage is straightforward: your real card number never reaches the merchant. When you pay with a virtual card, the merchant stores that virtual number. If the merchant suffers a data breach, attackers get a number that is either already expired, locked to that one merchant, or capped at a trivial dollar amount. Your actual bank account or credit line stays unexposed. Single-Use vs. Merchant-Locked Cards There are two main card types worth distinguishing. Single-use, or disposable, cards automatically "self-destruct" immediately after a single transaction. The card number becomes invalid the moment the merchant processes the payment. This is the strongest option for one-off purchases from unknown retailers. A merchant-locked card stays active over time but only works at one specific retailer. If you create a card tied to a streaming service, any attempt to charge that number at a different merchant gets declined automatically. This is particularly useful for managing subscriptions: you control exactly which vendor can bill you, and you can revoke the card instantly to cancel recurring charges without calling customer support or navigating cancellation pages designed to keep you subscribed. Pro Tip: When signing up for any free trial, generate a single-use card set to exactly $0 or $1. If the trial converts to a paid plan automatically, the charge will fail, no awkward cancellation call required. The Fraud Problem That Makes Burner Cards Necessary The Scale of Online Payment Fraud The risk of entering your real card number online is concrete and growing. eCommerce fraud in North America increased 207% between the first fiscal quarter of 2024 and 2025 Q1. That is not a gradual drift; it is an explosion. 43% of ecommerce consumers have been victims of payment fraud. If you shop online regularly, the statistical odds are not in your favor with a traditional card. The damage goes beyond the direct loss. Retailers ultimately lose $4.61 for every dollar of e-commerce fraud. Those costs flow back to consumers through higher prices and tighter return policies. The Capital One Shopping eCommerce Fraud Report also notes that 92% of stolen credit cards are accessed remotely, meaning the risk is almost entirely an online phenomenon, not physical theft. How Data Breaches Turn Your Real Card Against You When a retailer's database is breached, your real card number is one of thousands or millions exposed at once. With a real card, the fallout is significant: you have to cancel the card, update every saved payment method across streaming services, utilities, and subscriptions, and monitor for fraudulent charges for months. A disposable or one time card eliminates this cascade entirely. When your real card number leaks you deal with a replacement card, updated autopay settings across every service, and the anxiety of monitoring for fraudulent charges. With a virtual card, a breach at one merchant has zero impact on your other accounts or subscriptions because each merchant only ever saw an isolated number. The Subscription Trap Problem Fraud from unknown actors is only half the story. An FTC study of 642 subscription websites and apps found that 76 percent used at least one dark pattern, and 67 percent used more than one. These dark patterns are deliberate interface designs that make signing up effortless and canceling as difficult as possible. 81% of sites and apps studied used the technique of auto-renewing subscriptions automatically. The financial toll of forgotten subscriptions is substantial. According to SubBuddy's analysis of subscription trap data , the average household wastes $219 annually on unwanted subscriptions, and the FTC receives over 70,000 complaints yearly about subscription traps and auto-renewal issues. A burner credit card used for free trial signups completely sidesteps this problem, when the trial period ends, the disposable number is either already expired or can be cancelled with a single tap, regardless of how complicated the merchant's cancellation flow is. Pro Tip: Use a separate merchant-locked virtual card for every paid subscription. Set the spending limit to the exact monthly or annual charge. Any price increase attempt will decline automatically and land in your notification feed, giving you the choice to approve or cancel before a penny more leaves your account. How to Get and Use a Disposable Card Where to Get One Several options exist depending on what you already have. Many major card issuers and fintech services offer virtual cards. For example, Capital One has virtual cards through its Eno browser extension, Citi offers virtual account numbers in its online dashboard, and third-party services like Privacy.com can generate disposable card numbers. For consumers who want a virtual card tied to a budgeted balance rather than a linked credit line, dedicated budgeting tools with built-in virtual cards offer an alternative approach. Envelope combines virtual card functionality with envelope budgeting: each card is tied to a specific spending category and a pre-set balance, so the card itself enforces your budget. When the balance for that category runs out, the card declines, no overdraft, no overspend, and no real account number exposed to merchants. This makes Envelope's virtual cards a natural fit for anyone who wants both fraud protection and built-in spending discipline in one tool. People sometimes refer to virtual virtual credit cards, there are other providers that could work with your existing account. Click to Pay, for example, gives all Mastercard, Visa, Discover, and American Express cardholders access to virtual card numbers, regardless of their card's issuer. Step-by-Step: Using a Disposable Card for the First Time Log into your bank's app or dashboard, or sign up for a standalone service like Privacy.com. Generate a new card number. Set the spending limit to the exact amount of your planned purchase or the trial cost. Copy the generated card number, expiration date, and CVV. Enter those details at checkout exactly as you would enter a physical card. After the transaction, the single-use number is already invalid. For multi-use cards, freeze or delete the card from the app once the relationship ends. Almost all online retailers accept a virtual card, as it's processed like any other credit card transaction. The merchant cannot tell the difference between a disposable number and a permanent one. Limitations to Know Before You Start In my experience, the situations where virtual cards cause friction are predictable. Virtual cards aren't perfect for every situation. You can't use a virtual card at terminals that don't support mobile wallets. Some merchants still require a physical card. Hotels, rental car companies, and airlines frequently require a physical card for holds and pre-authorizations. Carry at least one physical card for travel even if you use disposable cards for everything online. Refunds deserve a quick note. If you buy something with a single-use virtual card, the number expires immediately, and then you need to return the item, refunds almost always still work. Your bank retains the virtual card data in its system even after the number is deactivated. When the merchant sends the refund to that old number, the bank recognizes it, matches it to your account, and credits the funds back. Choosing the Right Card for Each Situation A Practical Decision Guide Scenario Best Card Choice Why Buying from an unknown site once Single-use disposable card Number is dead before anyone can reuse it Free trial with credit card required Single-use card, $0-$1 limit Auto-renewal charge bounces Monthly software subscription Merchant-locked card, exact monthly amount Price increases fail automatically Budgeted shopping category Budgeted virtual card (e.g., Envelope) Spending hard-capped at your envelope balance Gift purchase (surprise) Any virtual card Real card never appears in shared accounts Common Mistakes That Undercut the Protection Pros: Your real account number is never exposed to any merchant A data breach at one retailer has zero impact on your other accounts Subscription auto-renewals fail when the disposable card expires You can freeze or delete a card instantly without canceling your main account Spending limits prevent charges from exceeding the approved amount Cons: Physical card still required for some in-person or travel use cases Single-use cards require generating a new number for every transaction Refunds occasionally need a manual reroute if the account is fully closed Some providers require linking a bank account or existing credit card first Not all international merchants accept every virtual card network Pro Tip: I've found that the most common mistake is setting a virtual card limit that's slightly too low and having a legitimate charge bounce at checkout. When setting limits for subscriptions, add a small buffer above the stated price to account for currency conversion or minor fee adjustments, something like $1-$2 above the displayed amount. Disposable Cards and Everyday Budgeting The fraud protection case for burner cards is clear. What is less discussed is their value as a budgeting tool. When you assign a virtual card to a specific spending category with a hard balance limit, the card itself becomes the enforcement mechanism. You do not need to check a spreadsheet or remember a mental budget, the card simply declines when the category runs out. This is the principle behind envelope budgeting, one of the most effective personal finance frameworks available. A virtual prepaid card is pre-funded, so it is designed for spending control: you can't spend more than you load. Envelope applies this directly: virtual cards are tied to individual budget envelopes, so your "dining out" card has its own balance, your "subscriptions" card has its own balance, and so on. When an envelope is empty, the associated card declines. This means your fraud protection and your spending discipline come from the same tool, with no extra setup required. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a disposable credit card and a regular virtual card? A regular virtual card may be multi-use and tied to a permanent card number relationship with a merchant. A disposable credit card, also called a one time use credit card or one time virtual card, generates a number that is only valid for a single transaction. Single-use cards automatically self-destruct immediately after a single transaction. The card number becomes invalid the moment the merchant processes the payment. Multi-use virtual cards remain active but can be locked to a specific merchant or spending limit. Is a burner credit card the same as a prepaid card? They are similar but structurally different. Virtual credit cards draw from a credit line, while virtual debit cards pull funds directly from your checking account. Virtual prepaid cards are loaded with money in advance and don't affect your credit. All three add security for online payments, but credit cards typically offer the most fraud protection and spending controls. A burner credit card is most often a virtual number tied to an existing credit account, whereas a prepaid virtual card is pre-funded independently. Will using a one time card affect my credit score? Using virtual or disposable card numbers does not affect your credit score by itself. The charges settle against your underlying credit account as normal, and your utilization and payment history are what determine your score, not whether you used a virtual number at checkout. If you are using a virtual prepaid card that is not credit-linked, there is no credit reporting at all. Can a merchant tell that I used a disposable card number? No. Almost all online retailers accept a virtual card, as it's processed like any other credit card transaction. The merchant sees a standard 16-digit card number, an expiration date, and a CVV. There is nothing in the transaction data that identifies the number as disposable or virtual. The merchant processes it identically to a physical card swipe. What happens to my money if I return something bought with a single-use card? Refunds almost always still work . Your bank retains the virtual card data in its system even after the number is deactivated. When the merchant sends the refund to that old number, the bank recognizes it, matches it to your account, and credits the funds back. In the rare case where the entire banking relationship has been closed, not just the virtual card number, the refund may bounce back to the merchant, who would then need to issue it by an alternative method. The Bottom Line Online fraud is not an edge case anymore. 43% of ecommerce consumers have been victims of payment fraud, and subscription trap designs mean that even legitimate merchants may charge you more than you agreed to. Disposable credit cards, one time virtual cards, and burner cards solve both problems with one mechanism: your real account number never reaches the merchant, so there is nothing to steal, and no way for an auto-renewal to hit a number that no longer exists. If you want the security of a burner card paired with a system that keeps your spending on budget at the same time, Envelope's virtual card feature ties each card to a specific budget envelope so the card itself enforces your spending plan. title: Polymath Robotics Blog | Case Study: Polymath Robotics and ConGlobal Collaboration
summary: Enabling Safe and Reliable Autonomous Terminal Operations
body_text: Photo courtesy ConGlobal Overview As the industry’s go-to expert in terminal operations, ConGlobal set the benchmark for innovation by showcasing the power of remotely operated hosters in terminal operations. To advance the safety of these remotely operated vehicles, ConGlobal partnered with Polymath Robotics to develop a sensor-based collision avoidance safety system. Through safe, reliable, and certifiable obstacle detection, ConGlobal and Polymath Robotics have laid the foundation to remove safety drivers through safe, reliable, and certifiable object detection. This partnership highlights how focused collaboration, and technical innovation can unlock safer, more efficient, and sustainable logistics solutions. The Challenge Remotely operated industrial vehicles can provide significant operational advantages, but they also have unique safety risks that must be mitigated. One such mitigation involves implementing deterministic, on-vehicle obstacle detection and collision avoidance that can satisfy applicable safety standards and enable the removal of safety drivers. The Solution Polymath Robotics implemented a robust safety architecture, focusing on three key components: On-Vehicle Sensor-Based Obstacle Detection Integrated sensors, including radar systems to detect obstacles, both large and small, in real-time. Optimized sensor placement and configuration to improve detection reliability for smaller objects, such as humans and cones. Achieved deterministic performance from radar systems, ensuring the ability to operate reliably in all weather and lighting conditions, ensuring safe operation in dynamic and unpredictable terminal environments. Controller-Level Safety Integration Developed an Obstacle Detection (OD) layer that integrated directly with the Vehicle Controller to ensure deterministic safety behavior. Enabled safe slowing and stopping operations within inches of target minimum braking distances. Path to Safety Certification Collaborated with a third-party safety reviewer to validate the system’s safety architecture. Built the solution within the criteria for safety certification, providing a clear, achievable path to satisfy applicable safety standards. On-vehicle, sensor-based obstacle detection Results The collaboration delivered tangible results for the safety of ConGlobal’s remotely operated hostlers: Safe Operation Demonstrated : The object detection system consistently met target braking distances and ensured safe operation around static and dynamic obstacles. Radar Optimization Success : Consistent detection of smaller objects, particularly humans, within challenging operational ranges. Path to Safety Certification : Polymath’s deterministic safety layer provided a clear path to achieving safety certification through third-party review. Optimized radar returns for consistent detection of objects within challenging operation ranges ‍ "At ConGlobal, we are continuously striving to push the boundaries of innovation in terminal operations. Our collaboration with Polymath Robotics on the Vehicle Safety System has been a critical step forward in our journey to enhance safety, efficiency, and sustainability in logistics. Together, we have laid the groundwork for a future where remote operations are not just a possibility, but a reality." – Brett Rogers, VP, Advanced Solutions ‍ A ConGlobal hostler avoids obstacles using Polymath's enhancements to the Vehicle Safety System Conclusion As the industry's go-to expert in terminal operations, ConGlobal set the benchmark for innovation by showcasing the power of remote operations. Polymath Robotics played a critical role in advancing the Vehicle Safety System by delivering a deterministic radar-based safety solution. Through safe, reliable, and certifiable obstacle detection, ConGlobal and Polymath Robotics have laid the foundation to remove safety drivers through safe, reliable, and certifiable object detection. This partnership highlights how focused collaboration, and technical innovation can unlock safer, more efficient, and sustainable logistics solutions. ‍
